paper.title: Good practice for evaluating predictions: what the literature supports

definitions.definition: A scoring function (an error measure for point forecasts) is consistent for a functional of the predictive distribution, such as the mean, the median or a quantile, when its expected value is lowest when the point forecast equals that functional.

A scoring rule for probabilistic forecasts is proper when its expected value is best when the forecast distribution equals the distribution of the outcome, and strictly proper when it is best only then.
A single-valued forecast meant to equal the mean (expected value) of the outcome's distribution given the information available.
A single-valued forecast meant to equal the median of the outcome's distribution given the information available.
Root mean squared error: the square root of the mean of the squared differences between outcomes and point forecasts.
Root mean squared scaled error: the RMSE of a series' forecasts divided by the in-sample RMSE of the one-step naive forecast of that series, so that series on different scales can be averaged.
Mean absolute error: the mean of the absolute differences between outcomes and point forecasts.
Mean absolute scaled error: the MAE of a series' forecasts divided by the in-sample MAE of the one-step naive forecast of that series.
Mean absolute percentage error: the mean of the absolute differences between outcomes and point forecasts, each divided by the outcome.
Symmetric mean absolute percentage error: the mean of the absolute differences between outcomes and point forecasts, each divided by the mean of the absolute outcome and the absolute forecast.
The beta-median with beta = -1: the point forecast that minimises the expected absolute percentage error; for positive outcomes it lies below the median.
The quantile (asymmetric piecewise linear) loss at level tau: tau times the error when the outcome is above the forecast, and (1 - tau) times the absolute error when it is below.
The score of a central (1 - alpha) prediction interval: its width plus 2/alpha times the distance by which the outcome falls outside it.
The share of outcomes that fall inside the prediction intervals, compared with their nominal level.
Continuous ranked probability score: the integral over thresholds of the squared difference between the forecast's cumulative distribution function and the step function at the outcome.
The logarithmic score: the negative logarithm of the forecast density (or probability) at the outcome.
The mean squared difference between forecast probabilities of a class and the outcome coded 1 if the class occurred and 0 otherwise.
The value of the forecast's cumulative distribution function at the outcome; for a calibrated forecast its values are uniformly distributed.
Statistical consistency between forecast distributions and outcomes: events forecast with a given probability occur with that frequency.
The concentration of the forecast distributions, a property of the forecasts alone; among calibrated forecasts, sharper ones are better.
The share of cases whose predicted class, after thresholding the predicted probabilities, equals the observed class.
The area under the ROC curve: the probability that a randomly chosen case of the positive class receives a higher score than a randomly chosen case of the negative class.
The curve of precision (the share of predicted positives that are positive) against recall (the share of positives predicted as positive) over the classification thresholds.
A time series with many zero values, such as the sales of a slow-moving item.
A non-parametric test of whether several methods differ, applied to their ranks on each of several data sets.
A post-hoc test after the Friedman test that compares every pair of methods by their mean ranks against a critical difference.
Multiple comparisons with the best: a test, on mean ranks over series, of which methods differ significantly from the best-ranked one.
A test of equal expected loss of two competing forecasts of the same series, based on the mean loss differential and its long-run variance.
Correcting a forecast back-transformed from a Box-Cox or log scale so that it estimates the mean, not the median, of the forecast distribution.
Exponential smoothing state space models with error, trend and seasonal components, each additive, multiplicative or absent.

claims.statement: Point forecasts should be evaluated with a [[D1:consistent scoring function]] for the functional they target: the mean, the median or a quantile.

about.subject: D1
conditions: the functional the forecasts target is known

claims.statement: [[D3:Point forecasts of the mean]] should be evaluated with squared error, as in [[D5:RMSE]].

When [[D3:point forecasts of the mean]] are compared over series on different scales, each series' [[D5:RMSE]] should be scaled by the in-sample RMSE of its one-step naive forecast, as in [[D6:RMSSE]].
[[D7:MAE]] and [[D8:MASE]] should not be the main measure for [[D3:point forecasts of the mean]].

about.relation: should not be the main measure for

claims.statement: [[D4:Point forecasts of the median]] should be evaluated with absolute error, as in [[D7:MAE]] or, across series on different scales, [[D8:MASE]].
On [[D24:intermittent series]], absolute-error measures should not be used alone.

about.subject: absolute-error measures
about.relation: should not be used alone on

claims.statement: Quantile forecasts should be evaluated with the [[D12:pinball loss]] at the quantile's level, averaged over the levels when there are several.
Prediction intervals should be evaluated with the [[D13:interval score]], reported together with their [[D14:coverage]] against the nominal level.
[[D14:Coverage]] alone should not be the measure of prediction intervals.

about.subject: D14
about.relation: should not be the only measure of

claims.statement: Predictive distributions should be evaluated with a [[D2:proper scoring rule]], such as the [[D15:CRPS]] or the [[D16:log score]].
The evaluation of predictive distributions should check their [[D19:calibration]] and report their [[D20:sharpness]].
Predictive distributions of counts, such as forecasts of intermittent sales, should be evaluated with proper scoring rules and a randomised [[D18:probability integral transform]].

about.subject: proper scoring rules and the randomised PIT

claims.statement: Forecast probabilities of classes should be evaluated with a [[D2:proper scoring rule]], such as the [[D16:log score]] or the [[D17:Brier score]].
[[D21:Accuracy]] should not be the measure of forecast class probabilities.

claims.statement: When the compared methods target different functionals, one the mean and another the median, each should be evaluated with a measure consistent for its own target, or the methods made to target the same functional.

about.subject: the comparison of methods with different targets

claims.statement: When methods are compared over many series, their accuracy should be summarised by the mean, the median and the quartiles of a scaled measure across the series, such as [[D6:RMSSE]] or [[D8:MASE]].

about.subject: aggregates of a scaled measure across series

claims.statement: To tell whether several methods whose aggregate accuracy is similar differ significantly over many series or data sets, their ranks on each series should be tested with the [[D25:Friedman test]] followed by [[D26:Nemenyi test]] post-hoc comparisons.

about.subject: D25
about.object: differences between methods of similar accuracy

claims.statement: To tell which methods differ significantly from the best one over many series, multiple comparisons with the best ([[D27:MCB]]) on ranks should be used.
The accuracy of two forecasts of the same series should be compared with the [[D28:Diebold-Mariano test]].
That a competition or a well-known study used an error measure should not be the reason for choosing it.

about.subject: the choice of an error measure by precedent

claims.statement: Scale-dependent error measures, such as [[D5:RMSE]] and [[D7:MAE]], should not be summed or averaged across series on different scales.

To aggregate the accuracy of point forecasts over series on different scales, each series' errors should first be scaled by a quantity of that series that does not depend on the compared forecasts, such as the in-sample error of its one-step naive forecast in [[D8:MASE]] or [[D6:RMSSE]], before the scaled errors are averaged.

about.subject: scaling per series before aggregation
about.object: accuracy over series on different scales

claims.statement: When quantile forecasts are compared over series on different scales, each series' [[D12:pinball loss]] should be scaled by a quantity of that series.

about.subject: D12

claims.statement: When prediction intervals are compared over series on different scales, each series' [[D13:interval score]] should be scaled by a quantity of that series.
